name: English
description: Words are your superpower—and this course helps you use them like a pro! You'll meet nouns, verbs, adjectives, and adverbs and see how they team up to make sentences pop. You'll become a reading detective, hunting for the main idea and getting to know story characters and settings. Then you'll write your own statements, questions, and exclamations and level up your spelling with short vowels, long vowels, blends, and compound words!

Every lesson is a chance to tell better stories, understand what you read, and spell with confidence. By the end, you'll have a whole toolkit of words and ideas—perfect for writing adventures, sharing your thoughts, and loving books even more.

lessons.title: Nouns
lessons.description: Learn about words that name people, places, and things.

sections.heading: What You'll Learn
body: In this lesson, you will learn about nouns — the words we use to name people, places, and things. Nouns are everywhere! By the end of this lesson, you'll be able to spot nouns in any sentence and even tell the difference between common and proper nouns.

sections.heading: Naming People and Places
body: A noun can name a person, like teacher, brother, or doctor. It can also name a place, like school, park, or city. Whenever you talk about someone or somewhere, you are using a noun!

sections.heading: Naming Things and Ideas
body: Nouns also name things you can touch, like book, apple, or chair. Some nouns name things you can't touch, like happiness, love, or freedom. These are called abstract nouns, and they name feelings or ideas.

sections.heading: What Are Common Nouns?
body: Common nouns are general names for people, places, or things. Words like dog, river, and city are common nouns. They do not start with a capital letter unless they begin a sentence.

sections.heading: What Are Proper Nouns?
body: Proper nouns name a specific person, place, or thing and always start with a capital letter. For example, Spot is a proper noun for a dog, the Mississippi is a proper noun for a river, and New York is a proper noun for a city. Remember: if it has a special name, capitalize it!

sections.heading: Noun Review
body: Remember, nouns name people, places, things, and ideas. Common nouns are general and lowercase, while proper nouns are specific and capitalized. Look around you right now — everything you see has a noun to name it!

question.text: Which of the following is a proper noun?

lessons.title: Verbs
lessons.description: Discover action words — run, jump, think, and more.

sections.heading: What You'll Learn
body: In this lesson, you will discover verbs — the action words that make sentences come alive! Verbs tell us what someone or something does. By the end, you'll be able to find verbs in sentences and use them to describe actions in the past, present, and future.

sections.heading: What Are Action Verbs?
body: Action verbs tell what someone or something does. Words like run, eat, sing, and write are all action verbs. If you can act it out with your body, it's probably an action verb!

sections.heading: Helping Verbs
body: Some verbs don't show action — they help the main verb instead. Words like is, am, are, was, were, has, and have are helping verbs. In the sentence "She is running," the word is helps the verb running.

sections.heading: Past, Present, and Future
body: Verbs change form to show when something happens. Present tense means it is happening now: "I walk." Past tense means it already happened: "I walked." Future tense means it will happen later: "I will walk."

sections.heading: Changing Verb Forms
body: To make most verbs past tense, add -ed to the end: jump becomes jumped, and play becomes played. Some verbs are tricky and change in a different way: run becomes ran, and eat becomes ate. These are called irregular verbs.

sections.heading: Verb Review
body: Verbs are words that show action or help other verbs. They can be in the past, present, or future tense. Every sentence needs at least one verb to be complete. Try clapping, jumping, or snapping — you just performed action verbs!

question.text: Which word is a verb in this sentence: "The cat jumped over the fence"?

lessons.title: Adjectives
lessons.description: Add describing words to make sentences more colorful.

sections.heading: What You'll Learn
body: In this lesson, you will learn about adjectives — the words that describe nouns and make your writing more interesting. Adjectives tell us what something looks like, feels like, or how many there are. By the end, you'll be adding adjectives to your sentences like a pro!

sections.heading: What Are Adjectives?
body: Adjectives are words that describe nouns. They answer questions like: What kind? How many? Which one? For example, in "the big red ball," the words big and red are adjectives that describe the ball.

sections.heading: Size, Shape, and Color
body: Some of the most common adjectives describe size, shape, and color. Think about a tiny round blueberry or a tall square building. These adjectives help the reader picture exactly what you're talking about.

sections.heading: Comparing Two Things
body: You can use adjectives to compare two things by adding -er to the end. A cheetah is faster than a turtle. A giraffe is taller than a horse. When you compare two things, you usually add -er and the word than.

sections.heading: Comparing Three or More
body: When you compare three or more things, add -est to the adjective. The cheetah is the fastest animal on land. Mount Everest is the tallest mountain in the world. The -est ending means something is the most of all!

sections.heading: Adjective Review
body: Adjectives describe nouns and make your writing more colorful. They tell about size, shape, color, number, and feelings. You can compare things with -er and -est endings. Try describing your favorite toy using at least three adjectives!

question.text: Which word is an adjective in this sentence: "She wore a sparkly dress"?

lessons.title: Adverbs
lessons.description: Learn words that tell how, when, or where something happens.

sections.heading: What You'll Learn
body: In this lesson, you will learn about adverbs — words that describe verbs, adjectives, or other adverbs. Adverbs tell us how, when, or where something happens. By the end of this lesson, you'll know how to spot adverbs and use them to add detail to your sentences.

sections.heading: Adverbs That Tell How
body: Many adverbs tell how something is done. These often end in -ly. For example: The turtle walked slowly. The girl sang loudly. The boy wrote neatly. The -ly ending is a big clue that a word might be an adverb!

sections.heading: Adverbs That Tell When and Where
body: Some adverbs tell when something happens, like today, yesterday, soon, and later. Others tell where, like here, there, outside, and everywhere. In the sentence "We played outside yesterday," both outside and yesterday are adverbs.

sections.heading: How Are They Different?
body: Adjectives describe nouns, but adverbs describe verbs. Compare these: "She is a quick runner" (quick describes the noun runner) and "She runs quickly" (quickly describes the verb runs). The trick is to ask: is it describing a thing or an action?

sections.heading: Using Adverbs in Your Writing
body: Adverbs make your writing more interesting by adding details. Instead of "The dog barked," try "The dog barked loudly." Instead of "She arrived," try "She arrived early." Adding an adverb helps the reader imagine the scene better.

sections.heading: Adverb Review
body: Adverbs describe verbs and tell how, when, or where something happens. Many adverbs end in -ly, but not all of them. Remember, adjectives describe nouns while adverbs describe verbs. Try adding an adverb to a sentence you say today!

question.text: Which word is an adverb in this sentence: "The rabbit hopped quickly across the yard"?

lessons.title: Finding the Main Idea
lessons.description: Figure out what a story or passage is mostly about.

pages.title: Welcome to Finding the Main Idea

sections.heading: What You'll Learn
body: In this lesson, you will learn how to find the main idea of a story or passage. The main idea is what the text is mostly about. By the end of this lesson, you'll be able to read a paragraph and quickly figure out its main idea.

sections.heading: The Big Picture
body: The main idea is the most important point the author wants you to understand. Think of it like the title of a movie — it tells you what the whole thing is about in just a few words. Every paragraph and every story has one main idea.

sections.heading: Main Idea vs. Details
body: Details are the smaller pieces of information that support the main idea. If the main idea is "Dogs make great pets," the details might be "Dogs are loyal," "Dogs love to play," and "Dogs can learn tricks." The details help explain or prove the main idea.

sections.heading: Look at the First and Last Sentences
body: Authors often put the main idea near the beginning or end of a paragraph. Try reading the first sentence and the last sentence carefully. One of them usually tells you what the whole paragraph is about.

sections.heading: Ask Yourself a Question
body: After you read, ask yourself: "What is this mostly about?" Try to answer in one short sentence. If your answer covers most of what you read, you found the main idea! If it only covers part, think bigger.

sections.heading: Main Idea Tips
body: To find the main idea, look at the first and last sentences, pay attention to repeated words, and ask yourself what the text is mostly about. The main idea is the big picture, and the details are the smaller pieces that support it.

question.text: Read this passage: "Bees are very important. They help flowers grow by spreading pollen. They also make honey that people enjoy." What is the main idea?

lessons.title: Story Characters
lessons.description: Get to know who the characters are and what they do.

sections.heading: What You'll Learn
body: In this lesson, you will learn about story characters — the people or animals in a story. You'll discover how to figure out what characters are like by paying attention to what they say, do, and feel. By the end, you'll be a character expert!

sections.heading: Finding the Characters
body: Characters are the people, animals, or creatures in a story. The main character is the one the story is mostly about. There are often other characters too, like friends, family, or even villains. To find the characters, ask: "Who is in this story?"

sections.heading: What Characters Do and Say
body: You can learn a lot about a character by watching what they do and listening to what they say. If a character shares their lunch, that shows they are kind. If a character tells a lie, that tells you something different. Actions and words are big clues!

sections.heading: Character Feelings
body: Characters have feelings just like real people. They might feel happy, scared, angry, or excited. Sometimes the author tells you how a character feels, and sometimes you have to figure it out from what happens in the story.

sections.heading: How Characters Change
body: In many stories, the main character changes from the beginning to the end. Maybe they start out scared and become brave, or they start out selfish and learn to share. Noticing how a character changes helps you understand the story's message.

sections.heading: Character Review
body: Characters are the people or animals in a story. You can learn about them by noticing what they say, do, and feel. Good readers pay attention to how characters change throughout the story. Next time you read, think about what makes each character special!

question.text: If a character in a story gives away their last cookie to a friend, what does that tell you about them?

lessons.title: Setting
lessons.description: Learn to identify where and when a story takes place.

sections.heading: What You'll Learn
body: In this lesson, you will learn about the setting of a story — where and when it takes place. The setting helps you picture the story in your mind. By the end, you'll be able to identify the setting in any story you read!

sections.heading: Where the Story Happens
body: The setting tells you where a story takes place. It could be a school, a forest, a castle, or even outer space! Authors use describing words to help you picture the place. Look for clues like names of places and descriptions of what things look like.

sections.heading: When the Story Happens
body: The setting also tells you when a story happens. It might take place in the morning, at night, in the summer, or long ago. Words like yesterday, in the future, or once upon a time are clues about when the story is set.

sections.heading: Setting Changes the Story
body: The setting can change how a story feels. A story in a dark, spooky forest feels very different from a story at a sunny beach. The setting affects the mood, or feeling, of the story. It also affects what characters can do.

sections.heading: Multiple Settings
body: Some stories have more than one setting. The characters might start at home, travel to school, and then go to the park. Each time the place or time changes, the setting changes too. Keep track of where and when the story moves!

sections.heading: Setting Review
body: The setting is where and when a story takes place. It helps you picture the story and affects how it feels. Look for clue words about places and times. A story can have one setting or many settings as the characters move around.

question.text: A story begins: "The snow fell softly outside the cabin in the mountains." What is the setting?
options: A cabin in the mountains in winter
question.answer: A cabin in the mountains in winter

lessons.title: Beginning, Middle, End
lessons.description: Every story has three parts — find them!

sections.heading: What You'll Learn
body: In this lesson, you will learn that every story has three parts: a beginning, a middle, and an end. Knowing these parts helps you understand and retell stories. By the end of this lesson, you'll be able to identify all three parts in any story!

sections.heading: The Beginning
body: The beginning of a story introduces the characters and the setting. It tells you who the story is about and where it takes place. The beginning also starts to show a problem or something interesting that gets the story going.

sections.heading: The Middle
body: The middle is the longest part of the story. This is where the main events happen and the characters try to solve a problem. Things might get harder before they get better. The middle is full of action and keeps you wanting to read more!

sections.heading: The End
body: The end of the story is where the problem gets solved and things wrap up. You find out what happens to the characters. The ending might be happy, surprising, or funny. A good ending makes you feel satisfied, like finishing a puzzle.

sections.heading: Retelling a Story
body: When you retell a story, use the beginning, middle, and end to keep things in order. Start by telling who the characters are and where the story happens. Then explain the main events. Finally, tell how it all ends. This helps others understand the story too!

sections.heading: Story Structure Review
body: Every story has a beginning, middle, and end. The beginning introduces characters and the setting. The middle has the main events and the problem. The end shows how the problem is solved. Use these three parts when you retell any story!

question.text: Which part of a story introduces the characters and setting?

lessons.title: What Makes a Sentence?
lessons.description: Every sentence needs a subject and a verb.

pages.title: Welcome to What Makes a Sentence?

sections.heading: What You'll Learn
body: In this lesson, you will learn what every sentence needs to be complete. A sentence must have a subject and a verb and express a complete thought. By the end of this lesson, you'll know how to tell the difference between a complete sentence and an incomplete one.

sections.heading: The Subject
body: The subject tells who or what the sentence is about. In the sentence "The dog barked," the subject is the dog. Every sentence needs a subject. Without one, the reader won't know who is doing the action.

sections.heading: The Predicate
body: The predicate tells what the subject does or is. It always includes a verb. In "The dog barked loudly," the predicate is barked loudly. Together, the subject and predicate make a complete sentence.

sections.heading: Complete Sentences
body: A complete sentence has a subject, a predicate, and expresses a whole thought. "The bird flew south" is a complete sentence. You know who did something (the bird) and what happened (flew south). It makes sense all by itself.

sections.heading: Fixing Fragments
body: A sentence fragment is a group of words that is missing a subject or a predicate. "Ran to the store" is a fragment because there is no subject. To fix it, add a subject: "Mom ran to the store." Now it's a complete sentence!

sections.heading: Sentence Review
body: Every complete sentence needs a subject and a predicate. The subject tells who or what, and the predicate tells what happens. If a group of words is missing one of these parts, it's a fragment and needs to be fixed.

question.text: Which of these is a complete sentence?

lessons.title: Statements
lessons.description: Write sentences that tell something and end with a period.

sections.heading: What You'll Learn
body: In this lesson, you will learn about statements — sentences that tell something. Statements share information and always end with a period. By the end of this lesson, you'll be writing clear, interesting statements of your own.

sections.heading: Telling Sentences
body: A statement is a sentence that tells you something. It shares a fact, an idea, or information. For example: "The Earth goes around the Sun." That sentence tells you a fact. Statements are the most common type of sentence you'll read and write.

sections.heading: Ending With a Period
body: Statements always end with a period — that little dot at the end of a sentence. The period tells the reader that the thought is complete. If you forget the period, your reader won't know where one thought ends and the next one begins.

sections.heading: Adding Details
body: A good statement gives the reader useful details. Compare these: "I have a pet" and "I have a fluffy orange cat named Whiskers." The second one paints a much better picture! Adding details like color, size, and names makes your statements more interesting.

sections.heading: Capitalization and Punctuation
body: Every statement starts with a capital letter and ends with a period. Check your writing by asking: Does it start with a capital? Does it end with a period? Does it express a complete thought? If you can say yes to all three, you wrote a correct statement!

sections.heading: Statement Review
body: Statements are telling sentences that share facts or information. They always begin with a capital letter and end with a period. Add details to make your statements more interesting. Practice by writing three statements about your favorite animal!

options: The library opens at nine o'clock.
question.answer: The library opens at nine o'clock.

lessons.title: Questions
lessons.description: Write sentences that ask something and end with a question mark.

sections.heading: What You'll Learn
body: In this lesson, you will learn about questions — sentences that ask for information. Questions always end with a question mark. By the end, you'll be able to write great questions and know the special words that start them.

sections.heading: What Is a Question?
body: A question is a sentence that asks something. It wants an answer! Questions end with a question mark (?), which looks like a little hook with a dot under it. When you read a question out loud, your voice usually goes up at the end.

sections.heading: Question Words
body: Many questions start with special words: who, what, when, where, why, and how. These words help you ask about different things. Who asks about a person. What asks about a thing. When asks about time. Where asks about a place. Why asks for a reason. How asks about the way something happens.

sections.heading: Writing Your Own Questions
body: To write a question, start with a question word or a helping verb like do, does, is, are, can, or will. Then add the rest of your thought and put a question mark at the end. For example: "Can birds fly at night?" or "Where do bears sleep in winter?"

sections.heading: Turning Statements Into Questions
body: You can turn a statement into a question by rearranging the words. The statement "She is going to the park" becomes the question "Is she going to the park?" Notice how the helping verb moved to the front. Don't forget to change the period to a question mark!

sections.heading: Question Review
body: Questions are sentences that ask for information and end with a question mark. Many start with who, what, when, where, why, or how. You can also turn statements into questions by moving the helping verb to the front. Try asking a friend three questions today!

question.text: Which of these is a question?
options: Where did you put my book?
question.answer: Where did you put my book?

lessons.title: Exclamations
lessons.description: Write exciting sentences that end with an exclamation point!

sections.heading: What You'll Learn
body: In this lesson, you will learn about exclamations — sentences that show strong feelings like excitement, surprise, or fear. Exclamations end with an exclamation point! By the end, you'll know when and how to use them in your writing.

sections.heading: What Is an Exclamation?
body: An exclamation is a sentence that shows a strong feeling. It might show excitement, surprise, anger, or joy. Exclamations end with an exclamation point (!). When you read one out loud, your voice gets louder or more emotional.

sections.heading: When to Use Exclamations
body: Use exclamations when something surprising, exciting, or important happens. "That was the best game ever!" shows excitement. "Watch out!" shows a warning. "I can't believe it!" shows surprise. Save exclamations for moments with real emotion — using too many can make them feel less special.

sections.heading: Making Your Exclamations Pop
body: Strong exclamations use powerful words that match the feeling. Instead of "That's nice!" try "That's incredible!" Instead of "I'm happy!" try "I'm thrilled!" Choosing the right words makes your exclamation really show how you feel.

sections.heading: Exclamations vs. Statements
body: A statement and an exclamation can say almost the same thing, but the feeling is different. "The roller coaster was fast" is a calm statement. "The roller coaster was so fast!" is an exclamation that shows excitement. The exclamation point changes everything!

sections.heading: Exclamation Review
body: Exclamations are sentences that show strong feelings and end with an exclamation point. Use them when something exciting, surprising, or important happens. Choose powerful words and don't overuse them. Practice by writing an exclamation about the best day you've ever had!

lessons.title: Short Vowel Words
lessons.description: Practice words like cat, bed, pig, hot, and bug.

sections.heading: What You'll Learn
body: In this lesson, you will learn about short vowel sounds. The vowels are a, e, i, o, and u, and each one has a short sound. By the end, you'll be able to read and spell lots of short vowel words like cat, bed, pig, hot, and bug.

sections.heading: What Are Short Vowels?
body: Every vowel has two sounds: a short sound and a long sound. The short a sounds like the a in cat. The short e sounds like the e in bed. The short i sounds like the i in pig. The short o sounds like the o in hot. The short u sounds like the u in bug.

sections.heading: CVC Words
body: Many short vowel words follow a pattern called CVC — consonant, vowel, consonant. The word cat is C-V-C: c is a consonant, a is the vowel, and t is a consonant. Other CVC words include map, hen, sit, mop, and cup. Knowing this pattern helps you spell new words!

sections.heading: Rhyming Short Vowel Words
body: Rhyming words end with the same sound. Cat rhymes with bat, hat, and mat. Bed rhymes with red, fed, and led. Rhyming helps you learn new words faster because you only need to change the first letter to make a new word!

sections.heading: Spelling Tips
body: When you hear a short vowel word, stretch it out slowly: c-a-t. Say each sound and write the letter that matches. If a word has three sounds and the middle one is a short vowel, it's probably a CVC word. Practice by writing word families like -at, -en, -ig, -op, and -ug.

sections.heading: Short Vowel Review
body: Short vowels make the sounds you hear in cat, bed, pig, hot, and bug. Many short vowel words follow the CVC pattern. Use rhyming to learn word families. The more you practice, the better you'll get at spelling short vowel words!

question.text: Which word has a short vowel sound?

lessons.title: Long Vowel Words
lessons.description: Learn words with silent e — like cake, bike, and home.

sections.heading: What You'll Learn
body: In this lesson, you will learn about long vowel sounds. When a vowel says its own name, like the a in cake or the i in bike, that's a long vowel sound. By the end, you'll know the silent e rule and be able to read and spell lots of long vowel words.

sections.heading: What Are Long Vowels?
body: A long vowel says its own name. The long a sounds like the a in cake. The long i sounds like the i in bike. The long o sounds like the o in home. When you hear a vowel saying its name in a word, you know it's a long vowel.

sections.heading: The Magic E
body: One of the most common ways to make a long vowel is by adding a silent e at the end of a word. The e doesn't make a sound — it's silent — but it makes the vowel before it say its name. Watch: cap becomes cape, bit becomes bite, and hop becomes hope. The silent e is like magic!

sections.heading: Two Vowels Working Together
body: Sometimes two vowels sit next to each other, and the first one says its name while the second stays silent. This is called a vowel team. In the word rain, the a says its name and the i is silent. Other examples are boat, leaf, and play.

sections.heading: Spelling Long Vowel Words
body: When spelling long vowel words, think about which pattern to use. Is it a silent e word like cake? Or a vowel team word like rain? Saying the word slowly and listening to the sounds will help you pick the right spelling. Practice makes perfect!

sections.heading: Long Vowel Review
body: Long vowels say their own name. The silent e at the end of a word makes the vowel before it long. Vowel teams are two vowels together where the first one is long and the second is silent. Remember: when two vowels go walking, the first one does the talking!

question.text: What happens when you add a silent e to the word "hop"?

lessons.title: Blends and Digraphs
lessons.description: Master sounds like bl, tr, sh, ch, and th.

sections.heading: What You'll Learn
body: In this lesson, you will learn about consonant blends and digraphs. Blends are two or three consonants that work together but keep their own sounds. Digraphs are two letters that team up to make one brand-new sound. By the end, you'll master sounds like bl, tr, sh, ch, and th!

sections.heading: What Are Blends?
body: A blend is two or three consonants that appear together in a word. You can hear each letter's sound when you say the blend. For example, in the word blue, you hear both the b and the l. In tree, you hear the t and the r.

sections.heading: Common Beginning Blends
body: Some blends you'll see a lot are bl (black), cl (clap), fl (flag), gl (glad), br (bring), cr (crab), dr (drum), fr (frog), gr (green), tr (train), sl (slide), sm (smile), sn (snap), sp (spin), and st (star). Try saying each one and listening for both sounds!

sections.heading: What Are Digraphs?
body: A digraph is two letters that join together to make one new sound. Unlike blends, you can't hear each letter separately. The letters sh make the sound you hear at the start of ship. The letters ch make the sound in chair. The letters th make the sound in think.

sections.heading: Digraphs at the Beginning and End
body: Digraphs can appear at the beginning or end of a word. You hear sh at the start of shoe and at the end of fish. You hear ch at the start of cheese and at the end of much. You hear th at the start of this and at the end of bath. Look for them everywhere!

sections.heading: Blends and Digraphs Review
body: Blends are consonants whose individual sounds you can still hear, like bl, tr, and st. Digraphs are two letters that make one new sound, like sh, ch, and th. Knowing these patterns helps you read and spell many new words. Listen carefully when you read — you'll hear blends and digraphs all around you!

question.text: Which word begins with a digraph?

lessons.title: Compound Words
lessons.description: Put two words together — sun + flower = sunflower!

sections.heading: What You'll Learn
body: In this lesson, you will learn about compound words — words that are made by putting two smaller words together. For example, sun + flower = sunflower! By the end, you'll be able to spot compound words, break them apart, and even make your own.

sections.heading: Two Words Become One
body: A compound word is a word made from two smaller words joined together. When you put the words cup and cake together, you get cupcake! The meaning of a compound word often comes from the two words inside it. A sunflower is a flower that faces the sun.

sections.heading: Compound Words Are Everywhere
body: You use compound words every day! Think about words like bedroom (bed + room), football (foot + ball), rainbow (rain + bow), and toothbrush (tooth + brush). Once you start looking, you'll find compound words in books, signs, and conversations.

sections.heading: Breaking Compound Words Apart
body: If you see a long word you don't know, check if it's a compound word. Try splitting it into two smaller words. The word starfish breaks into star and fish. The word notebook breaks into note and book. Breaking compound words apart can help you figure out what they mean.

sections.heading: Making New Compound Words
body: You can make compound words by combining small words. Try it! What happens when you put snow and man together? Snowman! What about basket and ball? Basketball! Some word combinations work and some don't, so always check if the compound word sounds right and makes sense.

sections.heading: Compound Word Review
body: Compound words are made by joining two smaller words together. You can break them apart to understand their meaning, and you can build new ones by combining words. Keep your eyes open for compound words — they're all around you in everyday life!

question.text: Which of the following is a compound word?
